title: The Long Road Home
author: Ada Tester
subtitle: A Memoir
dedication: For my mother, who kept the kitchen warm.
note: Model book 1 of 4 (rev 242): a book written in Inkhorse, shaped like a memoir. Original text written for Inkhorse's tests; not anyone's real book.
chapters:
I was born on a Tuesday in March, in a small hospital at the edge of a mill town, in a room that smelled of floor wax and coffee. My mother said later that it snowed all afternoon, and that my father drove home twice to make sure the furnace was still running.
The town sat on both banks of a slow brown river, and the newspaper on every porch was *L’Avenir National*. On the east side were the mills, tall brick buildings with rows of windows that caught the morning sun. On the west side were the houses, three stories high and close together, with porches stacked one above the other like shelves.
"You came early," my grandmother told me, years later. "Everything about you was early."
She meant it *kindly*. I think.
Our street ran uphill from the river to the church. At the bottom was a corner store that sold bread, newspapers, penny candy and, if you knew to ask, live bait. At the top was the parish hall, where every Friday night the whole neighborhood gathered for supper and cards and arguments about baseball.
# The House on Pine Street
We lived on the second floor of a gray house on Pine Street. The family who owned it lived below us, and an old man named Mr. Lavallée lived above. He played the violin badly every evening at six -- not well, not even nearly well, but with such devotion that nobody had the heart to complain.
My mother kept the kitchen warm from October to April. There was always a pot of something on the stove: soup, beans, or the thick pea soup her own mother had taught her to make, which took two days and could not be hurried.
I remember the radio on the windowsill, the sound of the trains crossing the river at night, and the way the frost made ferns on the glass. I remember my father coming home with sawdust in his hair. Most of all I remember the feeling that the whole world was exactly the size of that street, and that this was enough.
* * *
Memory is a strange archive. For years I believed that my uncle was born five years before me. Only recently, while sorting through a box of old papers, did I find his baptism certificate and realize that the years did not match. He was six years older, not five.
It is a small detail... and yet it changed how I understood a dozen stories I had told about us. We carry these little errors for decades, never questioning them, until one day we hold the paper in our hands.
And sometimes the smallest correction changes the whole picture.
A Family Between Two Countries, and the Long Road from Quebec to the Mill Towns of New England

For families like ours, the road from Quebec to New England was not a single journey but a long migration, repeated by cousins and neighbors over sixty years. They came for work in the mills, and they brought their language, their parishes and their recipes with them.
My great-grandparents crossed the border in 1910 with two trunks, a sewing machine and a letter from a priest. The letter said that Léon was an honest man and a good worker, which was true, and that he spoke some English, which was not.
They settled in a neighborhood where nobody needed English anyway. The butcher spoke French, the doctor spoke French, the newspaper was printed in French. On Sundays the sermon was in French, and the hymns were the same ones they had sung at home.
"We did not *leave* home," my great-grandmother used to say. "We brought it with us, one piece at a time."
# Work and Wages
The mills ran six days a week. A weaver in 1915 earned about nine dollars for a fifty-four hour week, and children as young as fourteen worked beside their parents on the looms. The noise was so loud that workers learned to read each other's lips.
My great-grandfather worked in the dye house, where the floors were always wet and the air was thick with steam. He came home every night with his hands stained blue or red or green, depending on the order of the day, and my grandmother remembered that you could tell the season's fashions by the color of his fingers.
By 1925 he had saved enough to buy a small house on the hill. It had a garden, a cellar for potatoes and a view of the river. He planted tomatoes, beans and a single apple tree, which was still bearing fruit when I was a boy.
It is hard to explain what that house meant to them. It was proof that the long road had been worth walking.

The bridge across the river was built in 1937, of steel and concrete, with lamps along both sides that were lit by hand every evening. Before the bridge, the only way across was a ferry that ran from six in the morning until nine at night, weather permitting.
My father loved that bridge. On summer evenings he would walk me down to the middle of it, lift me up onto the railing and hold me there, both hands around my waist, while we watched the water slide past underneath.
"Look at it," he would say. "It never stops. Not for anybody."
I did not understand what he meant until much later, after he was gone, when I stood on the same bridge by myself and watched the river go by -- brown and patient and unstoppable, exactly as he had said.
* * *
Some places stay with us long after we leave them. The bridge is one of those places for me. When I close my eyes I can still feel the cold iron under my hands, hear the hum of the cars on the deck behind us, and smell the river: mud and leaves and something like rain.
I have crossed many bridges since then, some of them famous, some of them very long. None of them has ever felt quite like that one.
Perhaps that is what home means: not the place itself, but the way it keeps its hold on you, year after year, no matter how far you travel.
